bio:
Riccardo Guidotti is an Associate Professor at the Department of Computer Science of the University of Pisa and a member of the Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining Laboratory (KDDLab), a research group in collaboration with ISTI-CNR of Pisa and Scuola Normale Superiore.

He graduated with honors in Computer Science from the University of Pisa, where he obtained both his Bachelor's and Master's degrees and later earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science with a thesis on "Personal Data Analytics". He won the IBM fellowship program and worked at IBM Research in Dublin, Ireland, in 2015. He also received the DSAA New Generation Data Scientist Award in 2018 and the Marco Somalvico Award for Artificial Intelligence in 2021.

His research interests include explainable artificial intelligence, interpretable machine learning, personal data mining, clustering, and the analysis of transactional data and time series.

Anna Monreale is an Associate Professor at the Department of Computer Science of the University of Pisa and a member of the Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining Laboratory (KDDLab), a joint research group with the Information Science and Technology Institute of the National Research Council in Pisa.

Her research interests include big data analytics, social networks, and privacy issues arising from the analysis of social and human-sensitive data. In particular, she works on the evaluation of privacy risks in analytical processes and on the design of privacy-by-design technologies for big data.

She earned her Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Pisa in 2011 with a dissertation on privacy-by-design in data mining.

Mattia Setzu is an Assistant Professor at the Department of Computer Science of the University of Pisa and a member of the Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining Laboratory (KDDLab).

His research focuses on explainable artificial intelligence, with particular attention to explanations for tabular and textual data. He graduated summa cum laude in 2018 and obtained his Ph.D. in Computer Science in 2022 with a thesis titled "Opening the Black Box: Empowering Machine Learning Models with Explanations".

His work on explainability includes decision trees, their expressive power, and their adaptation to non-relational data. In natural language processing, he has worked on authorship attribution and on fairness in language models, studying possible causes of unfair behavior.

Francesco Spinnato is an Assistant Professor (RTD-A) at the University of Pisa. He earned his Bachelor's degree in Economics and Management from the University of Padua in 2017 and his Master's degree in Data Science from the University of Pisa in 2020. He obtained his Ph.D. in Data Science from Scuola Normale Superiore in 2024.

His research focuses on explainable artificial intelligence applied to sequential data, with particular attention to the interpretation of black-box models for univariate and multivariate time series. In 2024, he collaborated with the Visualization and Data Analytics (VIDA) Research Center at New York University.

He received the 2023-2024 Socint G-Research Italian National Prize for his Ph.D. thesis, "Explanation Methods for Sequential Data Models".

Alessandro Berti is a postdoctoral researcher in quantum computing at the University of Pisa.

His interests include innovation, technology, and quantum computing. In 2019, he started PointerPodcast, a podcast focused on innovation and technology. In the same year, he started Tocket, a startup project on blockchain-based ticketing aimed at countering ticket scalping.

In 2020, he founded Superhero Valley, a community designed to help students prepare for interviews at major technology companies.

Cristiano Landi is a postdoctoral researcher at the Department of Computer Science of the University of Pisa and a member of the Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining Laboratory (KDDLab), a research group in collaboration with ISTI-CNR of Pisa and Scuola Normale Superiore.

He earned his Master's degree in Data Science and Business Informatics from the University of Pisa in 2022 with a thesis on "Interpretable Machine Learning Models for Trajectory Classification". He also holds a Bachelor's degree in Computer Science from the same university.

His research focuses on alternative data representations for improving the performance of state-of-the-art machine learning models. He has collaborated with the Data Science Lab at the University of Piraeus on mobility data representation for sub-trajectory clustering. His broader research interests include mobility data analytics, explainable and interpretable artificial intelligence, and human-centered artificial intelligence.

Martina Cinquini is a Research Fellow and a Ph.D. candidate in Computer Science at the University of Pisa, supervised by Professors Riccardo Guidotti and Salvatore Ruggieri.

She earned her Master's degree in Data Science and Business Informatics from the University of Pisa in 2021 with a thesis on "Boosting Synthetic Data Generation with Effective Nonlinear Causal Discovery". She also holds a Bachelor's degree in Digital Humanities from the same university, which she completed with honors in 2017.

Her research focuses on methodologies that discover and exploit causal knowledge to uncover and prevent discrimination and to promote the interpretability of machine learning models. She has collaborated with institutions including INRIA in France and Saarland University in Germany, working on advanced causal analysis techniques for fairness in artificial intelligence and dynamic systems.

Alessio Cascione is a PhD student in the Italian National PhD Program in Artificial Intelligence. He holds a graduate degree in Digital Humanities from the University of Pisa.

His research interests focus on explainable machine learning, with particular attention to case-based reasoning approaches for the development of interpretable-by-design models.

He is also interested in natural language processing, especially for the detection of harmful online content. He holds a Bachelor's degree in Philosophy from the University of Pisa, where he focused on philosophy of language, philosophical logic, and epistemology.

Alessandro Poggiali holds a PhD in Artificial Intelligence at is a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Pisa.

His research interests focus on quantum machine learning. He has a strong academic background in artificial intelligence and is committed to advancing research on quantum-enhanced artificial intelligence.

Andrea Fedele received his Ph.D. from the National Ph.D. Program in Artificial Intelligence for Society at the University of Pisa. He also holds a Master's degree in Data Science and Business Informatics from the University of Pisa and a Bachelor's degree in Computer Science from the University of Salerno.

His research focuses on human-centered artificial intelligence, with particular attention to explainability, interpretability, and trustworthiness. He is especially interested in the interpretability of few-shot learning models, developing both post-hoc explainers and interpretable-by-design architectures.

He also works on the trustworthiness of artificial intelligence systems in relation to the requirements introduced by the AI Act.

Marta Marchiori Manerba is an external collaborator of the group. She holds a Ph.D. in Artificial Intelligence within the National PhD Program, in the Artificial Intelligence and Society area.

Her work focuses on fairness and explainability in natural language processing, with particular attention to digital discrimination and algorithmic bias. During her studies, she explored the relationship between technology and human rights. She also holds a Bachelor's degree in Digital Humanities from the University of Pisa, where she developed an interest in hate speech detection against minorities in online discourse.

Her research interests include natural language processing, responsible language technologies, human-centered artificial intelligence, explainability, transparency, fairness, algorithmic auditing, machine learning evaluation, data awareness, intersectionality, digital discrimination, and abusive language detection.
